Former Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA) (NYSE: BRKB) CEO Warren Buffett made several incredible investments. However, he was also noteworthy for letting some obvious ones get away.

One of those was Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), which he regretted not buying sooner. However, he remedied that mistake by purchasing shares not long before leaving his role. Current CEO Greg Abel has kept purchasing Alphabet shares, showing that he's also bullish on the stock.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Another stock that Buffett identified as a major value opportunity right away was Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) in the mid-2010s. This turned out to be one of Buffett's best investments ever, and while Berkshire has sold off the number of Apple shares it owns compared to its peak holdings, it's still the largest position in its portfolio.

The question is, between the two, which one is the better buy now? I think it's Alphabet, but the answer to that question may depend on whether you're bullish on AI or not.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Alphabet is going all-in on AI

Alphabet and Apple are taking two distinct approaches to the emerging AI landscape. Alphabet is going all-in on AI, and plans to spend about $200 billion on data center capital expenditures this year. The uses for these data centers range from being rented out via its cloud computing unit (a very profitable endeavor) to being used for compute capacity for its Gemini platform (not profitable right now). Regardless, Alphabet has positioned itself as an AI-first investment, but there are those who may be a bit wary regarding Alphabet's all-in position on an emerging technology.

Apple is taking the complete opposite approach. Instead of rapidly increasing its AI computing power, it's choosing to deploy Google's Gemini model on its devices, cutting development costs substantially. While it will have to pay to utilize Gemini, the cost to develop a new model may have been far higher in infrastructure and research and development (R&D) expenses. Furthermore, the AI features that Apple has rolled out are lackluster to some, although the revamped Siri AI is receiving positive reviews. Apple still has a long way to go before AI is a top product, and it could lose market share in the smartphone market to some Android phones that are pioneering this technology.

Shares of HubSpot (NYSE:HUBS) charged sharply higher on Thursday, surging as much as 7%. As of 2:44 p.m. ET, the stock was still up 6.1%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The catalyst that sent the cloud-based customer relationship management (CRM) specialist higher was chatter about recent mergers and acquisitions and what it could mean for the future.

Image source: Getty Images.

It only takes a spark

A wave of recent acquisitions in the software space has Wall Street analysts speculating about the future, and HubSpot came up in the conversation.

Earlier this week, Salesforce announced its intention to acquire Braze, a leading customer engagement platform, in a deal valued at $5.66 billion, representing a 58% premium over the prior day's closing price. This marked the third such major acquisition of a small- to mid-cap software company in recent weeks.

Just last week, cloud software and artificial intelligence (AI) company CCC Intelligent Solutions agreed to be taken private by a group of private investment firms including GTCR and Elliot Investment Management for $6.1 billion, marking a 44% premium. On the same day, cybersecurity provider Varonis Systems agreed to be acquired by privately held competitor Proofpoint for $6.3 billion, a 52% premium to the stock price prior to the rumored sale.

In the wake of this tidal wave of merger mania, Jefferies analyst Samad Samana has surveyed the landscape and believes there are more deals to come. He posits that the Braze buyout could be the "the spark that could lead to a strategic takeout" of rival Klaviyo. The analyst goes on to suggest that while he views an acquisition of HubSpot as unlikely, the company could be an attractive candidate for private equity.

Acquiring HubSpot would be a more costly affair, as the company has a market cap of more than $13 billion (as of this writing) -- and that doesn't include any premium shareholders would require to approve such a deal. Assuming the average premium of 51% for the above-cited deals, any acquisition of HubSpot would be in the neighborhood of $20 billion.

Like many software-as-a-service (SaaS) stocks, HubSpot has been punished in recent years as investors feared competition from AI, though the reality has proven to be more complicated. However, with the stock price near a five-year low, HubSpot could be an attractive acquisition for a company with deep pockets.

Tuesday evening, Netflix delivered a solid third-quarter financial report for fiscal 2026, posting $12.87 billion in revenue -- an 11.9% year-over-year increase. Operating income rose by 34.6% and net income jumped 43.9%. Free cash flow ticked 8.4% higher, amounting to 86% of earnings and 25% of revenue.

Despite these strong operating metrics, Wall Street kind of hated the release. Major financial institutions such as Barclays and Goldman Sachs lowered their price targets, while Needham downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold. Netflix's stock price also dropped as much as 6.7% on Wednesday morning.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Netflix.

A solid quarter that Wall Street hated

The negative sentiment was driven mostly by weaker-than-expected full-year advertising revenue guidance plus lingering concerns over U.S. content comparisons. Every year can't match 2025's game-changing home runs like 2025's K-Pop Demon Hunters, after all.

When a stock pulls back and massive share repurchases surge in tandem, conventional wisdom whispers that management must be backing up the wagon to load up on deeply discounted equity. Both of those components are certainly in play right now.

The buyback illusion: Are insiders signaling incredible value?

During the third quarter, Netflix executed its largest quarter of share buybacks in company history, repurchasing 63.9 million shares for $4.8 billion and bringing its year-to-date buybacks to $10.8 billion. However, that doesn't necessarily mean that Netflix's management sees exceptional value in its own stock today.

A massive capital return program alongside a depressed share price might traditionally be interpreted as an aggressive, valuation-driven signal from management. Still, historical execution patterns suggest a different reality for Netflix. Rather than acting as nimble, valuation-conscious tacticians swooping in during sell-offs, Netflix's capital return program behaves more like a systematic machine.

Netflix's massive free cash flow generation simply hits pre-set programmatic targets, meaning heavy buying often coincides with cyclical peaks just as easily as troughs.

For example, take a look at the historical timeline: when Netflix shares crashed through the floorboards in 2022, buybacks practically dried up into a tiny puddle just when the stock was actually cheap. Then they surged to record highs in mid-2026 as the stock pulled back from prior peaks.

If there's one thing the AI industry-complex needs more of, according to Jensen Huang, it's money.

On Thursday, the perpetually leather-clad CEO of Nvidia told CNBC that the one thing holding neoclouds back is "working capital" to meet claimed demand.

"If you look at the fundamentals, the demand for the neo clouds is off the charts ... [but] what is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth," Jensen said from the GTC conference in Berlin. "Because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital."

This is coming from someone whose company, Nvidia, is currently worth $5.14 trillion and has risen almost 1,000% over the last five years, and who is referring to a sector that has already surpassed the scale of the late-1990s dot-com and telecom boom. This is coming from someone whose portfolio company Nscale, a British neocloud startup, just got ditched by Microsoft because it didn't have the power to run the GPUs in the data centers for inference. This is coming from someone one of whose biggest AI company customers for chips, OpenAI, is burning billions, warning of possible mass extinction and doesn't expect to be profitable (maybe) until 2030.

Scarcity of capital hasn't been a problem. Neocloud startups have raised approximately $24.6 billion across 83 recorded financings in 2025 and 2026 so far, according to New Market Pitch. What Jensen may actually be referring to is that capital investment in European neoclouds so far isn't enough, or, to use his word, "scarcity."

"Across all of Europe, you're going to need a lot more neo clouds," he stated.

From a business perspective, this makes sense. Nvidia's entire thing is supplying neoclouds with GPU racks filled with its chips, regardless of whether, once they're in there, the data center actually has the power to run them. To be fair, that's none of Jensen's business. It is his business when neoclouds stop buying, because once that happens, the entire AI flywheel ceases to rotate.

Turning trash into cash

Waste Connections' third-quarter revenue rose 7% year over year to $2.6 billion.

The trash collector employs a growth-through-acquisition business model, enabling it to steadily expand its waste services network. The acquisitions it completed so far this year are projected to add roughly $130 million in annualized revenue.

Additionally, Waste Connections' focus on exclusive and secondary markets gives it strong pricing power, allowing it to increase its fees above the rate of inflation. These price hikes have helped to offset rising fuel costs as diesel prices have spiked.

All told, Waste Connections' adjusted net income increased 7% to $399 million. Its earnings per share, boosted by stock buybacks, climbed 10% to $1.58. That topped Wall Street's estimates, which had called for per-share profits of $1.52.

Rising profits mean larger dividends for shareowners

These solid results prompted Waste Connections to lift its full-year financial forecast. Management now expects revenue of $10.1 billion, net income of $1.2 billion, and adjusted free cash flow of more than $1.4 billion.

The landfill operator also raised its quarterly dividend by 10% to $0.385 per share.

"The strength of our operating performance, free cash flow generation, and balance sheet positioned us for another double-digit annual increase in our quarterly cash dividend, our sixteenth in a row," CEO Ronald Mittelstaedt said.
